summary: Corrects the ABNF rule for IPv6 literals in RFC 3261 and clarifies how to compare URIs containing textual IP addresses. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A grammar mistake in how addresses were written got fixed so programs read them correctly.

questions: sip uri comparison with ip addresses
how are sip uris with ipv6 addresses compared
subtitle: A fix for a faulty IPv6 grammar rule in SIP, plus a rule that URIs compare by binary address, not by spelling.

tldr.problem: The grammar in RFC 3261 for IPv6 literals can generate a malformed address with an extra colon, and SIP had no rule for comparing URIs whose IP addresses are written differently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC replaces the IPv6address and IPv4address rules with the ones from RFC 3986, and changes the URI comparison rule so hosts match when different text yields the same binary IP address.
tldr.outcome: SIP implementations get a correct grammar and a clear equality rule for addresses. The document updates RFC 3261.

today: RFC 5954 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3261. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This Correction Is
sections.content:
This document corrects the Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF) production rule that RFC 3261 (SIP) uses for generating IPv6 literals. It also clarifies how Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) are compared when they contain textual representations of IP addresses.

It is a short, targeted patch and formally updates RFC 3261.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small repair to an older rulebook. One rule for writing addresses was wrong, and another rule about when two addresses count as the same was missing.

sections.title: The Extra Colon Bug
sections.content:
The ABNF for IPv6 literals in RFC 3261 is incorrect. When generating IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses it can produce [2001:db8:::192.0.2.1], with an extra colon before the IPv4 part. The correct form has only two colons there.

The cause is in the IPv6address rule, which prefixes IPv4address with a : token. Two alternatives of the hexpart rule already end with ::, so adding another colon gives the faulty result. The RFC says this ABNF was derived from Appendix B of RFC 2373, which was flawed to begin with. RFC 2373 was later obsoleted by RFC 4291.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule sometimes let you write an address with one colon too many, like typing a double comma in a sentence. The result looked fine to the rule but was not a real address.

sections.title: The Grammar Fix
sections.content:
The fix is to use the IPv6address rule from Appendix A of RFC 3986. This document reproduces it, along with h16, ls32, IPv4address and dec-octet.

The update to RFC 3261 is:

  • The RFC 3261 IPv6address and IPv4address rules MUST NOT be used. The same-named rules from RFC 3986 MUST be used.
  • This makes the hexpart, hexseq and hex4 rules from RFC 3261 obsolete, so they MUST NOT be used.

A side effect is that the stricter IPv4address rule no longer allows syntactically valid but semantically invalid SIP URIs such as sip:bob@444.555.666.777.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of patching the broken rule, the authors swap in the correct version that another rulebook already has. Impossible addresses like 444.555.666.777 also stop being allowed.

sections.title: Comparing URIs With IP Addresses
sections.content:
SIP compares URIs for many reasons. For example, registrars compare them when they receive a binding update. Section 19.1.4 of RFC 3261 said that for two URIs to be equal, the user, password, host and port components must match. That leaves a question when the same IPv6 address is written differently, such as sip:bob@[2001:db8::9:1] and sip:bob@[2001:db8::9:01]. They look different as text but are binary equivalents.

The same ambiguity exists for IPv4 (is 192.0.2.128 equal to 192.00.02.128?), but IPv6 compressed notation and hybrid addresses make it more acute.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing 7 and 07 uses different letters for the same number. The old rule did not say whether a computer should treat those as the same address or different ones.

sections.title: The New Comparison Rule
sections.content:
The text says it is the binary equivalence of the IP address that must be considered. Section 19.1.4 of RFC 3261 is modified. The old rule (user, password, host and port components must match) gets this addition: if the host contains a textual IP address that may vary in representation, the host components match if the different textual representations yield the same binary IP address.

The RFC also requires adding examples to Section 19.1.4 of RFC 3261. The following pairs are equivalent:

  • sip:bob@[::ffff:192.0.2.128] and sip:bob@[::ffff:c000:280]
  • sip:bob@[2001:db8::9:1] and sip:bob@[2001:db8::9:01]
  • sip:bob@[0:0:0:0:0:FFFF:129.144.52.38] and sip:bob@[::FFFF:129.144.52.38]

This applies to textual forms of both IPv6 and IPv4 addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The new rule says to compare where the address points, not how it is spelled. If two spellings point to the same place, they match.

sections.title: Canonical IPv6 Text and Security
sections.content:
Implementers SHOULD generate IPv6 text representations as defined in RFC 5952, which keeps the output consistent. Section 3.2 of this RFC also points readers there for recommendations on IPv6 text.

On security, the RFC says it introduces no new considerations beyond those in RFC 3261.
sections.plainLanguage: When writing out an address, people should use the standard tidy spelling so everyone writes it the same way. This fix does not create any new security problems.

viz.caption: OLD AND NEW SECTION 19.1.4 COMPARISON RULE (RFC 5954, SECTION 4.2)

data.title: Rule text
data.code:
OLD:
For two URIs to be equal, the user, password, host, and port
components must match.

NEW:
For two URIs to be equal, the user, password, host, and port
components must match.  If the host component contains a textual
representation of IP addresses, then the representation of those
IP addresses may vary.  If so, the host components are considered
to match if the different textual representations yield the same
binary IP address.
